children: Despite a perception among US law students that politics plays a key role in judicial clerk hiring, judges themselves say political ideology is not a top factor, according to a new study on how judges pick their clerks.
Instead, judges say they seek to identify law students and recent law graduates who can meet their demands while getting along with everyone and ideally forming lifelong relationships.

Judicial clerkships are highly sought-after one-year positions working under the mentorship of a judge, often helping to research and draft opinions. Clerkships can significantly boost a newly minted lawyer's pedigree, opening doors to prestigious jobs in law firms, law schools and government.

According to the new study titled What Judges Want, based on interviews with 194 federal and state judges, clerkship hiring appears less like a “political animal at work” and more akin to “putting together a jazz quintet.”
“The quintet needs players with skill, who can get along while being stuck in a small room, and who will come back for the reunions,” the study reads.

The study by Vanderbilt law professor Tracey George, University of Virginia law professor Mitu Gulati and University of Toronto law professor Albert Yoon builds upon their previous work highlighting the rise of judicial clerkship “stacking” — where law graduates complete two, three, or even four coveted clerkships with sitting judges before entering the legal workforce.
That trend is concentrating clerkship opportunities among a small pool of candidates and shrinking the pool of clerkships available to others, they found.

While many law students perceive politics to be a “key ingredient” in the clerkship hiring process, the professors wrote in their latest study, none of the interviewed judges said they would only hire clerks who are members of the conservative Federalist Society or the left-leaning American Constitution Society.
Only 39% raised politics or ideology as factors in clerk hiring but none said they hire clerks expressly for shared politics.

The judges said they rely heavily on recommendations from trusted law professors or other judges, with some reporting they cannot trust law school grades to identify who will be a good addition to their chambers. Experience and maturity were top factors.

Many judges reported enjoying lifelong relationships with their former clerks, from officiating their weddings to meeting their children, who are referred to as “grand clerks,” according to the study.
“In many cases, judges are choosing confidants for life,” it said.
